newsitem.title: INDIA: Open India-Pakistan commerce routes, traders urge.
newsitem.headline: Open India-Pakistan commerce routes, traders urge.

text.p: On the 50th anniversary of their countries' independence, traders in India and Pakistan have pressed for land routes between them to be opened to boost commerce, business leaders said on Thursday.
Bilateral trade between the two arch-rivals is channelled through a twice-weekly rail link between Amritsar in India and Lahore in Pakistan and a land border crossing at Wagah in Amritsar.
Indian traders say increased trade between the two neighbours would be mutually beneficial.
India and Pakistan traded goods and services directly worth $110 million while trade through third countries was estimated between $225 million and $450 million in 1995-96 (April-March).
Increased trade would help India to earn more foreign exchange and Pakistan to cut prices of essential commodities, said Indrajit Sachdeva, joint secretary of the Amritsar Chamber of Commerce.
"If the government lifts the restrictions on export items and opens the land route today exports would double immediately," Sachdeva told Asian News International (ANI).
"Since there are many restrictions, exports today are limited to about 5.0 billion rupees ($138 million). We have to now depend on the only available railway route for export," he added.
Indian exporters complain border trade between India and Pakistan which started in 1977 has not increased significantly because not enough railway wagons are available.
Opening up the land route is the only way to boost it, they say.
Apart from the rail service, porters carry goods from either side of the border and hand them over to their counterparts at the Wagah border check-post, manned by security personnel.
In March this year India and Pakistan resumed a dialogue that collapsed in January 1994 over the disputed Himalayan territory of Kashmir.
Senior diplomats of the two countries held talks in New Delhi and Islamabad and set up working committees aimed at moving forward the dialogue on outstanding issues, including cross-border trade.
Indian and Pakistani foreign ministers also met in April during the Non-Aligned Movement conference in New Delhi.
Later, Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and his Pakistani counterpart Nawaz Sharif met at a summit of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) in the Maldives in May.
The South Asian countries last year agreed on a SAARC preferential trading arrangement (SAPTA), which essentially means trading concessions among the seven member countries.

But Pakistan's hesitation to accord most-favoured nation status to India has been stalling implementation of SAPTA and the realisation of achieving a South Asian Free Trade Agreement or SAFTA by the year 2000.
India and Pakistan have gone to war three times since independence from Britain in 1947, twice over Kashmir.
